title: A Square and A Cube
subject: Maths-1
description: Perfect squares and cubes, their digit and factor patterns, square and cube roots by prime factorisation and estimation, and the history of varga, ghana and mula.

questions.question: A locker is open at the end of the process only if the number of times it is toggled is
questions.explanation: Every locker starts closed. Each toggle flips it, so an odd number of toggles leaves it open and an even number leaves it closed. 'A multiple of 2' is just another way of saying even.

questions.question: Why does locker 36 remain open at the end?
options: 36 is a multiple of 6, so Person 6 is the last to touch it
36 is toggled by exactly two people, Persons 1 and 36
36 has an odd number of factors, because 6 pairs with itself
36 has an even number of factors, because 1 pairs with 36
questions.explanation: Factors come in partner pairs (1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9) except 6×6, where the partner is the same number. So 36 has 9 factors — odd — and is toggled 9 times, ending open.

questions.question: How many of the 100 lockers remain open at the end?
questions.explanation: Only lockers whose numbers are perfect squares stay open: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100 — ten lockers.

questions.question: The passcode 2-3-5-7-11 came from the first five lockers touched exactly twice. These locker numbers are all
questions.explanation: A locker is touched once for each factor of its number. Exactly two touches means exactly two factors (1 and itself) — the definition of a prime.

questions.question: Suppose the same puzzle is played with 200 people and 200 lockers. How many lockers stay open?
questions.explanation: Open lockers are the perfect squares up to 200. Since 14² = 196 ≤ 200 but 15² = 225 > 200, there are 14 such lockers.

questions.question: What is the final state of locker 12, and why?
questions.explanation: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — six of them, an even count — so it is toggled six times and ends closed. 12 is not a perfect square, so no factor pairs with itself.

questions.question: Every number has an even number of factors.
questions.explanation: False. Perfect squares such as 1, 4, 9, 36 have an odd number of factors because one factor pairs with itself (for example 6 × 6 = 36).

questions.question: A locker whose number has exactly 3 factors, such as locker 49, remains open at the end.
questions.explanation: True. 49 has factors 1, 7 and 49 — three toggles, an odd number — so it ends open. Having exactly three factors means the number is the square of a prime.

questions.question: Which statement about the locker puzzle is NOT correct?
options: Locker 1 is toggled only once, by Person 1 alone
Locker 100 is toggled 9 times and ends open
Locker 50 is toggled 6 times and ends closed
Locker 64 ends closed because 64 is an even number
questions.explanation: Parity of the locker number is irrelevant; what matters is the count of factors. 64 = 8² has 7 factors (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64), so it is toggled 7 times and ends OPEN. The other statements are correct: 1 has one factor, 100 has nine, 50 has six.

questions.question: Select all the lockers that remain open at the end of the puzzle.
questions.explanation: Only perfect-square lockers stay open: 16 = 4² and 64 = 8². 18, 72 and 50 are not squares, so each has an even number of factors and ends closed.

questions.question: The area of a square whose side is 3/5 unit is
questions.explanation: Area = side × side = (3/5) × (3/5) = 9/25. Both numerator and denominator are squared; 6/10 is a common slip from doubling instead of squaring.

questions.question: Why are the numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, … called square numbers?
options: Each has exactly four factors, matching the four sides of a square figure
Each can be drawn as a square figure whose side is exactly one unit long
Each is the perimeter of a square figure that has a whole-number side
Each is the number of unit squares that fill a square with a whole-number side
questions.explanation: A square of side n units contains n × n unit squares — its area. So 1, 4, 9, 16 are the areas of squares with sides 1, 2, 3, 4. Perimeters would be 4, 8, 12, 16, and 9 has three factors, not four.

questions.question: Which of these numbers is NOT a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 15² = 225 and 16² = 256, so 226 lies strictly between consecutive squares and cannot be a square — even though it ends in 6. 169 = 13², 196 = 14², 256 = 16².

questions.question: The area of a square field is 441 m². The length of its side is
questions.explanation: Side = √441 = 21 m because 21 × 21 = 441. Check: 20² = 400 and 22² = 484, so 21 is the only fit.

questions.question: Which of the following equations is correct?
questions.explanation: 17 × 17 = 289. The others are miscalculations: 18² = 324, 19² = 361 and 21² = 441.

questions.question: Since 6.25 is the square of 2.5, it is a perfect square.
questions.explanation: False. 6.25 is a square, but 'perfect squares' are defined as squares of natural numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, …). 2.5 is not a natural number.

questions.question: How many perfect squares have exactly two digits?
questions.explanation: Two-digit squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 (squares of 4 to 9) — six of them. 1, 4, 9 have one digit and 100 has three.

questions.question: The largest perfect square less than 1000 is
questions.explanation: 31² = 961 and 32² = 1024 > 1000, so 961 is the largest square below 1000. 900 = 30² is smaller, and 999 ends in 9 but is not a square.

questions.question: Select all expressions whose value is 12².
questions.explanation: 12² means 12 × 12 = 144. Writing '122' or adding/doubling to get 24 are common slips — the small 2 is an exponent, not a digit.

questions.question: In the row 3, 6, 10, 15, 1 every adjacent pair adds to a square. Select the adjacent pairs whose sum is 16.
questions.explanation: 6 + 10 = 16 and 15 + 1 = 16. The other adjacent pairs also give squares, but different ones: 3 + 6 = 9 and 10 + 15 = 25.

questions.question: Which digits can NEVER appear in the units place of a perfect square?
questions.explanation: Squaring the digits 0–9 gives units digits 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1 only. So 2, 3, 7, 8 never occur; 4, 6, 8 are not all excluded because 4 and 6 do occur.

questions.question: Which one of these numbers is a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 2032, 2048 and 1027 end in 2, 8 and 7, digits no square can end with. 1089 = 33² (33 × 33 = 1089).

questions.question: A number ends in the digit 6. Which conclusion is correct?
options: It is definitely a perfect square
It is definitely not a perfect square
It is a perfect square only if it is even
It may or may not be a perfect square
questions.explanation: 16 and 36 end in 6 and are squares, but 26 also ends in 6 and is not. The units digit can only rule a square OUT (digits 2, 3, 7, 8); it can never confirm one.

questions.question: Which of these squares does NOT have 6 in the units place?
questions.explanation: The units digit of a square depends only on the units digit of the number. 4² = 16 and 6² = 36 end in 6, so 34², 46², 56² end in 6; but 2² = 4, so 82² = 6724 ends in 4.

questions.question: Which of these squares have 4 as their last digit? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Only the units digit matters: 8² = 64 and 2² = 4 end in 4, so 108² and 292² end in 4. Both 64² and 36² end in 6 because 4² = 16 and 6² = 36.

questions.question: If a number has 9 in its units place, its square ends in
questions.explanation: 9 × 9 = 81, so any number ending in 9 has a square ending in 1 — the same as numbers ending in 1, since 1 × 1 = 1.

questions.question: The squares 1², 9², 11², 19², 21² and 29² all end in 1. The NEXT two squares ending in 1 are
questions.explanation: A square ends in 1 exactly when the number ends in 1 or 9. After 29 the next such numbers are 31 and 39 (31² = 961, 39² = 1521). 41 comes after 39, not before.

questions.question: Every perfect square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, and every number ending in one of these digits is a perfect square.
questions.explanation: False. The first half is true, but the converse fails: 26 ends in 6 and 10 ends in 0, yet neither is a square.

questions.question: Which statement about units digits of squares is NOT correct?
options: The units digit alone can prove that a number is NOT a square
Squares of numbers ending in 4 or 6 always end in the digit 6
Squares of numbers ending in 1 or 9 always end in the digit 1
The units digit alone can prove that a number IS a square
questions.explanation: A units digit of 2, 3, 7 or 8 proves 'not a square', but a 'good' units digit proves nothing — 26 is the chapter's counter-example. The patterns for 4/6 → 6 and 1/9 → 1 are genuine.

questions.question: Which number ends in a digit that squares CAN have, and yet is not a square?
questions.explanation: 26 ends in 6, a digit squares may have, but 5² = 25 and 6² = 36 leave no room for 26 to be a square. 16, 25 and 36 are 4², 5², 6².

questions.question: If a number has 3 zeros at the end, how many zeros will its square have at the end?
questions.explanation: Trailing zeros double on squaring: (a × 1000)² = a² × 1 000 000. For example 7000² = 49 000 000 has six zeros.

questions.question: Judging only by the trailing zeros, which of these could be a perfect square?
questions.explanation: A square has an even number of trailing zeros. 810000 has four (and is 900²). 8100000 has five, 100000 has five and 49000 has three — all odd, so none is a square.

questions.question: The square of an even number is
questions.explanation: An even number has a factor 2, so its square has a factor 4 and is even. Parity is preserved: even² is even and odd² is odd.

questions.question: Which statement about trailing zeros is correct?
options: A square has double the trailing zeros of the number squared
A square has the same trailing zeros as the number squared
A square has half the trailing zeros of the number squared
A square always has exactly two zeros at the end of it
questions.explanation: 100² = 10000 (2 → 4 zeros), 7000² = 49 000 000 (3 → 6 zeros). Each trailing zero is a factor of 10, and squaring multiplies by 10 twice for each.

questions.question: A perfect square can end with exactly three zeros.
questions.explanation: False. The trailing zeros of a square are twice those of its root, so their count is always even: 0, 2, 4, 6, …

questions.question: The square of an odd number is always odd.
questions.explanation: True. odd × odd = odd. For example 7² = 49, 11² = 121, 25² = 625.

questions.question: 700² = 490000 has 4 zeros at the end. How many zeros will 70000² have at the end?
questions.explanation: 70000 has 4 trailing zeros, so its square has 2 × 4 = 8: 70000² = 4 900 000 000.

questions.question: Which of these is definitely NOT a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 2500000 has five trailing zeros — an odd count, impossible for a square. The others have an even count and are squares: 250000 = 500², 25000000 = 5000², 2500 = 50².

questions.question: If n² is an odd number, what can be said about n?
options: n must be an even number
n may be even or odd
n must be a prime number
n must be an odd number
questions.explanation: Even numbers have even squares, so an odd square can only come from an odd n. Being odd does not make n prime (9² = 81 is odd).

questions.question: Select the numbers that could be perfect squares, judging by their trailing zeros.
questions.explanation: Squares need an even number of trailing zeros: 40000 (four zeros, = 200²) and 6400 (two zeros, = 80²). 4000 has three zeros and 640 has one.

questions.question: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 equals
questions.explanation: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n². Here there are 7 terms, so the sum is 7² = 49.

questions.question: The nth odd number is
questions.explanation: Odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, …: the 1st is 2(1) − 1 = 1, the 6th is 2(6) − 1 = 11. 2n + 1 would make the 1st odd number 3.

questions.question: Given 35² = 1225, which number must be added to 1225 to get 36²?
questions.explanation: 1225 is the sum of the first 35 odd numbers; adding the 36th odd number, 2 × 36 − 1 = 71, gives 36² = 1296. (Equivalently 35 + 36 = 71.)

questions.question: Given 125² = 15625, the value of 126² is
questions.explanation: 126² = 125² + (126th odd number) = 15625 + (2 × 126 − 1) = 15625 + 251 = 15876. 253 is the 127th odd number and 126 is just the number itself.

questions.question: Subtracting 1, 3, 5, … from 38 gives 37, 34, 29, 22, 13, 2, −11. What does this show?
options: 38 is a sum of 7 odd numbers
questions.explanation: A perfect square is reduced to exactly 0 by subtracting consecutive odd numbers from 1. 38 skips 0 (2 then −11), so it is not a sum of the first few odd numbers — not a square.

questions.question: 50 can be written as a sum of consecutive odd numbers starting from 1.
questions.explanation: False. Only perfect squares can be written this way, and 50 lies between 7² = 49 and 8² = 64. (1 + 3 + … + 13 = 49; adding 15 gives 64.)

questions.question: Given 50² = 2500, what is 49²?
In the pattern 4² + 5² + 20² = (___)², the missing number is
questions.explanation: 16 + 25 + 400 = 441 = 21². In this pattern the third number is the product of the first two (4 × 5 = 20) and the answer is one more than it.

questions.question: In the pattern 1² + 2² + 2² = 3², 2² + 3² + 6² = 7², 3² + 4² + 12² = 13², the missing numbers in 9² + 10² + (___)² = (___)² are
questions.explanation: The third number is the product of the first two: 9 × 10 = 90. The right side is that product plus one: 91. Check: 81 + 100 + 8100 = 8281 = 91².

questions.question: Select the sums that equal a perfect square.
questions.explanation: Consecutive odd numbers STARTING FROM 1 sum to a square: 1+3+5+7 = 16 = 4² and 1+…+11 = 36 = 6². 3+5+7 = 15, 1+3+5+9 = 18 (skips 7) and 5+7+9 = 21 are not squares.

questions.question: How many numbers lie between 16² and 17²?
questions.explanation: Between n² and (n+1)² there are 2n numbers: 2 × 16 = 32. (17² − 16² − 1 = 289 − 256 − 1 = 32.)

questions.question: How many numbers lie between 99² and 100²?
If p and q are consecutive perfect squares (p < q), the number of numbers strictly between them is
questions.explanation: Counting from p + 1 up to q − 1 gives q − p − 1 numbers; q − p counts one of the endpoints as well.

questions.question: How many perfect squares lie between 101 and 200?
questions.explanation: 121, 144, 169 and 196 (squares of 11 to 14). 100 and 225 fall outside the block.

questions.question: How many perfect squares lie between 901 and 1000?
questions.explanation: Only 961 = 31². 900 = 30² is just below the block and 1024 = 32² is above it. Squares thin out as numbers grow.

questions.question: The sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is always
options: a number that is a cube
questions.explanation: 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 6 = 9, 6 + 10 = 16, 10 + 15 = 25: two consecutive triangles fit together to form a square.

questions.question: Which pair of consecutive triangular numbers adds up to 36?
questions.explanation: Triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, … and 15 + 21 = 36 = 6². The pairs 10 + 15 = 25 and 21 + 28 = 49 give other squares.

questions.question: Between which pair of consecutive squares are there exactly 50 numbers?
questions.explanation: Between n² and (n+1)² there are 2n numbers, so 2n = 50 gives n = 25: between 625 and 676 there are 50 numbers. Between 50² and 51² there are 100.

questions.question: Moving from one pair of consecutive squares to the next, the count of numbers between them increases by 2.
questions.explanation: True. The count is 2n, so it goes 2, 4, 6, 8, … — between 1 and 4 there are 2 numbers, between 4 and 9 there are 4, and so on.

questions.question: Select the correct sums of consecutive triangular numbers.
If y = x², then x is called
questions.explanation: Taking the square root undoes squaring: since 7² = 49, 7 is the square root of 49.

questions.question: The integer square roots of 64 are
questions.explanation: 8 × 8 = 64 and (−8) × (−8) = 64, so both are square roots. 4 and 16 are factors of 64 (4 × 16 = 64) but not its roots, since 4² = 16 and 16² = 256.

questions.question: Why does every perfect square have two integer square roots?
options: Every square can be split into two equal halves
A negative integer times itself is also a positive square
Every perfect square has an even number of factors
Squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, giving two possibilities
questions.explanation: x² = (−x)², so both x and −x square to the same number: 8² = 64 and (−8)² = 64. In this chapter only the positive root is used.

questions.question: The area of a square is 1296 cm². Its side is
questions.explanation: 36² = 1296 (the chapter computes 36² = 1225 + 71). 34² = 1156 and 38² = 1444 do not match, and 46² ends in 6 but equals 2116.

questions.question: Why is listing squares one by one considered an inefficient way to find a square root?
options: For large numbers far too many squares must be computed
It can never find the square root of an odd number
It only works for numbers that end in the digit 6
It produces the negative root instead of the positive
questions.explanation: To check 576 we computed squares from 21 to 24, but a number like 15625 would need over a hundred squares. Prime factorisation or estimation is faster.

questions.question: Can 327 be a perfect square?
options: No, because it ends in the digit 7
No, because 327 is an odd number
questions.explanation: No square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8, so 327 is ruled out immediately. Odd numbers can be squares (9, 25) and nearness to 324 proves nothing.

questions.question: Square root is the inverse operation of squaring.
questions.explanation: True. Squaring 9 gives 81 and taking the square root of 81 gives back 9.

questions.question: The square root of 576 can be found by subtracting 1, 3, 5, … successively and counting that 0 is reached at the 24th step.
questions.explanation: True. 576 = 24², and 24² is the sum of the first 24 odd numbers, so exactly 24 subtractions reach 0. It works, but it is slow for big numbers.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a square root of 100?
questions.explanation: 10² = 100 and (−10)² = 100, so 10 (written +10 or 10) and −10 are the square roots. 50 is half of 100, a common confusion between halving and rooting.

questions.question: Select the TRUE statements about √49 = 7.
options: A square of area 49 sq cm has side 7 cm
−7 is also a square root of 49
questions.explanation: Side = √area, so a 49 sq cm square has side 7 cm, and (−7)² = 49 makes −7 a root too. 49 is the SQUARE of 7, and 7 is not a cube root of 49 (7³ = 343).

questions.question: 324 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. Therefore √324 =
questions.explanation: Group the factors into two identical sets: (2 × 3 × 3) × (2 × 3 × 3) = 18 × 18, so √324 = 18. Taking one of each prime (2 × 3 = 6) or all the 3s (27) is a slip.

questions.question: Why is 156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13 not a perfect square?
options: The factors 3 and 13 cannot be paired
It has an odd number of factors
It has four prime factors in total
The prime 2 appears twice in it
questions.explanation: A square needs every prime to appear an even number of times. The 2s pair up, but 3 and 13 each appear once. Having four prime factors or a repeated 2 is fine (36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 is a square).

questions.question: Is 1156 a perfect square?
options: No, because it ends in the digit 6

questions.question: 2800 = 2⁴ × 5² × 7. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A perfect square, because every exponent is even
Not a perfect square, because it ends in 00
Not a perfect square, because 7 is unpaired
questions.explanation: 2⁴ and 5² pair up, but the single 7 cannot. Ending in 00 is actually consistent with a square; the exponent of 7 is 1, which is odd.

questions.question: The smallest number by which 9408 must be multiplied so that the product is a perfect square is
questions.explanation: 9408 = 2⁶ × 3 × 7². Only the 3 is unpaired, so multiplying by 3 makes every prime appear an even number of times.

questions.question: After multiplying 9408 by 3 we get 28224. Its square root is
The smallest square number divisible by each of 4, 9 and 10 is
questions.explanation: LCM(4, 9, 10) = 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. The lone 5 must be paired, so the smallest square multiple is 180 × 5 = 900 = 30². 3600 works but is not the smallest.

questions.question: Why must 180, the LCM of 4, 9 and 10, be multiplied by 5 (not 2 or 3) to get the smallest square?
options: 5 is the largest prime factor that appears here
180 is not a multiple of 5 × 5 = 25, so it fails
questions.explanation: In 180 the primes 2 and 3 already appear in pairs; the single 5 is the only obstacle, so ×5 is both necessary and sufficient. 6 is not a prime, so the last reasoning is invalid.

questions.question: The smallest number by which 2800 must be DIVIDED to get a perfect square is
questions.explanation: 2800 = 2⁴ × 5² × 7. Removing the unpaired 7 gives 400 = 20². Dividing by 28 also leaves a square (100), but 7 is the smallest divisor that works; dividing by 70 leaves 40, which is not a square.

questions.question: The smallest number by which 156 must be multiplied to make it a perfect square is
questions.explanation: 156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13; both 3 and 13 are unpaired, so we need 3 × 13 = 39. Then 156 × 39 = 6084 = 78². Multiplying by 3 or 13 alone leaves one prime unpaired.

questions.question: Which of these prime factorisations represent perfect squares? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 = 10² and 2 × 3 × 3 × 2 = 36 = 6² have every prime an even number of times. The others have an odd count of 2, 3 or 5.

questions.question: √1936 lies between 40 and 50 because
options: the number 1936 ends in the digit 6
questions.explanation: Bracketing with known squares: 1600 = 40² is below 1936 and 2500 = 50² is above it, so the root is between 40 and 50. The units digit tells us about the LAST digit of the root, not its size.

questions.question: Using (40 + 5)² = 40² + 2 × 40 × 5 + 5², the value of 45² is
questions.explanation: 1600 + 400 + 25 = 2025. Forgetting the middle term 2 × 40 × 5 = 400 gives 1625.

questions.question: Since 45² = 2025 is greater than 1936, √1936 must be
questions.explanation: The root lies between 40 and 45 and ends in 4 or 6; the only candidate is 44. Check: 44² = 1936.

questions.question: √250 is approximately 16 (slightly less) because
options: 250 ends in 0, so its root is even
questions.explanation: 250 is 6 away from 16² = 256 and 25 away from 15² = 225, so the root is nearer to 16 — but still a little below it, since 250 < 256.

questions.question: Akhil's square cloth has area 125 cm². Can he cut a square handkerchief of side 15 cm from it?
options: No, since 125 is not a multiple of 15
questions.explanation: A 15 cm square needs 225 cm² of cloth, but only 125 cm² is available. Comparing 15 with the area 125 mixes up length and area.

questions.question: The largest square handkerchief with an integer side that can be cut from a 125 cm² square cloth has side
questions.explanation: 11² = 121 ≤ 125 but 12² = 144 > 125, so 11 cm is the biggest whole-number side that fits.

questions.question: To the nearest whole number, √700 is
questions.explanation: 26² = 676 and 27² = 729. 700 is 24 above 676 and 29 below 729, so it is nearer 26. (35 is 700 ÷ 20, not a root.)

questions.question: To the nearest whole number, √1500 is
questions.explanation: 38² = 1444 and 39² = 1521. 1500 is 56 above 1444 but only 21 below 1521, so it rounds to 39.

questions.question: Because 1936 ends in 6, its square root must be 46.
questions.explanation: False. A final digit of 6 only narrows the root to 44 or 46. Since 45² = 2025 > 1936, the root is below 45, so √1936 = 44.

questions.question: Select the TRUE statements about √250.
options: It is closer to 16 than to 15
questions.explanation: 225 < 250 < 256 puts the root between 15 and 16, and 250 is nearer 256, so it is nearer 16. It is not exactly 15.5 (15.5² = 240.25) and it is below 20 since 20² = 400.

questions.question: How many cubes of side 1 cm are needed to make a cube of side 3 cm?
questions.explanation: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27: three layers, each a 3 × 3 square of 9 unit cubes. 9 is one layer; 81 is 3⁴.

questions.question: A cube of edge 4 units contains 64 unit cubes because
options: 4 is added 16 times to count every cube in the solid
each layer has 4 cubes and there are 16 such layers
each layer has 4 × 4 = 16 cubes and there are 4 layers
it has 6 faces with 4 cubes each, plus cubes inside
questions.explanation: Layer by layer: a 4 × 4 square of 16 unit cubes, stacked 4 high, gives 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

questions.question: 12³ equals
questions.explanation: 12 × 12 = 144 and 144 × 12 = 1728. 1444 is 38², and 1278 just rearranges digits.

questions.question: Which digits can appear in the units place of a perfect cube?
questions.explanation: Cubing 0–9 gives last digits 0, 1, 8, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 9 — every digit occurs. Unlike squares, no digit is ruled out.

questions.question: (−6)³ equals
questions.explanation: (−6) × (−6) = 36 and 36 × (−6) = −216. An odd number of negative factors keeps the sign negative, unlike (−6)² = 36.

questions.question: How many perfect cubes have exactly 3 digits?
questions.explanation: 125, 216, 343, 512 and 729 (cubes of 5 to 9). 64 has two digits and 1000 has four.

questions.question: No number from 10 to 26 is a perfect cube.
questions.explanation: True. 2³ = 8 and 3³ = 27, so there are no cubes between them.

questions.question: A perfect cube can end with exactly two zeros.
questions.explanation: False. Each trailing zero of a number becomes three in its cube (10³ = 1000), so cubes end in 0, 3, 6, 9, … zeros — never exactly two.

questions.question: Why can a perfect cube never end with exactly two zeros?
options: A cube can never end with the digit zero at all
Cubes of even numbers always end in the digit 8
Trailing zeros of a cube always come in pairs
Trailing zeros of a cube come in groups of three
questions.explanation: n = a × 10ᵏ gives n³ = a³ × 10³ᵏ, so the count of trailing zeros is a multiple of 3 (0, 3, 6, …). Pairs of zeros belong to squares.

questions.question: Which statement about cubes is NOT correct?
options: The cube of a 2-digit number may be a 3-digit number
The cube of an odd number is always an odd number
A perfect cube may end with the digit 8, like 2³
The cube of a negative number is always negative
questions.explanation: The smallest 2-digit number is 10 and 10³ = 1000 already has 4 digits, so a 2-digit cube has 4 to 6 digits (99³ = 970299). The other statements are true.

questions.question: Which is the greatest: 67³ − 66³, 43³ − 42³, 67² − 66² or 43² − 42²?
questions.explanation: Consecutive cubes differ far more than consecutive squares, and the gap grows with size: 67³ − 66³ = 13267, 43³ − 42³ = 5419, 67² − 66² = 133, 43² − 42² = 85.

questions.question: 3375 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 5. Therefore ∛3375 =
questions.explanation: Split into three identical groups: (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) = 15³, so the cube root is 15.

questions.question: Why is 500 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5 NOT a perfect cube?
options: The three 5s appear too many times
500 is even, and cubes are never even
It has only two different prime factors
The two 2s cannot form a group of three
questions.explanation: A cube needs every prime in triplets. The 5s form a triplet, but only two 2s are present. Having two primes is fine (3375 = 3³ × 5³).

questions.question: ∛27000 equals
questions.explanation: 27000 = 27 × 1000 = 3³ × 10³ = 30³. Three trailing zeros in the number become one zero in the root.

questions.question: ∛10648 equals
questions.explanation: 10648 ends in 8, so the root ends in 2 (2³ = 8). Also 8 < 10.648 < 27 puts the tens digit at 2. Check: 22³ = 10648.

questions.question: 1323 = 3³ × 7². By what smallest number should 1323 be multiplied to make it a perfect cube?
questions.explanation: The 3s already form a triplet; the 7s need one more to make 7³. 1323 × 7 = 9261 = 21³.

questions.question: Compared with the number itself, each prime factor appears in the prime factorisation of its cube
questions.explanation: 6 = 2 × 3 gives 6³ = 2³ × 3³; 12 = 2² × 3 gives 12³ = 2⁶ × 3³. Every exponent is multiplied by 3, not increased by 3.

questions.question: You are told 1331 is a perfect cube. Without factorising, its cube root is
questions.explanation: 1331 ends in 1, so the root ends in 1; and 1 < 1.331 < 8 means the tens digit is 1. So ∛1331 = 11.

questions.question: ∛4913 equals
questions.explanation: 4913 ends in 3; only 7³ = 343 ends in 3, so the root ends in 7. Since 1 < 4.913 < 8, the tens digit is 1: the root is 17.

questions.question: The smallest number by which 500 must be multiplied to get a perfect cube is
questions.explanation: 500 = 2² × 5³ has only two 2s; one more 2 completes the triplet: 500 × 2 = 1000 = 10³. Multiplying by 4 gives 2000 = 2⁴ × 5³, not a cube.

questions.question: A number is a perfect cube if its prime factors can be split into three identical groups.
questions.explanation: True. 3375 = (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) = 15³ is the chapter's example.

questions.question: 'Cube numbers have an odd number of factors.' Which judgement is correct?
options: True; every cube is also a perfect square
False; every cube has exactly three factors
questions.explanation: Only perfect squares have an odd number of factors. 8 has 4 factors and 27 has 4 (1, 3, 9, 27). Some cubes, like 64 = 8², happen to be squares too, but not all.

questions.question: 7 + 9 + 11 = 27 = 3³. Which sum of consecutive odd numbers gives 4³?
questions.explanation: n³ is a sum of n consecutive odd numbers, continuing where the previous group stopped: after 11 come 13, 15, 17, 19 and 13 + 15 + 17 + 19 = 64 = 4³.

questions.question: 91 + 93 + 95 + … + 109 (ten consecutive odd numbers) equals
questions.explanation: In the pattern 1, 3+5, 7+9+11, … the group of 10 odd numbers sums to 10³ = 1000. Quick check: ten numbers averaging 100 give 1000.

questions.question: 1729 is called the Hardy–Ramanujan number because
options: it was the number of Ramanujan's hospital room in Cambridge
it is the smallest number that is a sum of two squares in two ways
Hardy proved that it was the largest possible taxicab number
it is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two ways
questions.explanation: Hardy's taxi was numbered 1729; Ramanujan instantly noted 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³, the smallest such number.

For perfect squares, the successive differences become constant after how many levels, and with what value?
questions.explanation: Level 1 differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, … and level 2 differences are all 2.

questions.question: For perfect cubes 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216 the successive differences become constant at
questions.explanation: Level 1: 7, 19, 37, 61, 91. Level 2: 12, 18, 24, 30. Level 3: 6, 6, 6. One extra level compared with squares, and the constant is 3! = 6.

questions.question: Taxicab numbers are numbers that can be expressed as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.
questions.explanation: True. 1729, 4104 and 13832 are the first three; the name comes from Hardy's taxi numbered 1729.

questions.question: Hardy told Ramanujan that 1729 was a very interesting number.
questions.explanation: False. Hardy called 1729 'rather a dull number'; it was Ramanujan who replied that it was very interesting.

questions.question: 67² − 66² equals
questions.explanation: The difference of consecutive squares is the next odd number, 2n − 1 with n = 67, i.e. 133 = 67 + 66.

questions.question: Select all the expressions equal to 1729.
The first known lists of perfect squares and cubes, from around 1700 BCE, were compiled by
questions.explanation: Babylonian clay tablets listed squares and cubes to speed up finding square and cube roots.

questions.question: In ancient Sanskrit works, the term varga was used for
options: only the root of a plant and the root of a number
only the fourth power, called the square of a square
both the square figure (or its area) and the square power
only the solid cube and the third power of a number
questions.explanation: Varga meant the square figure, its area and also the square of a number — showing the square power has its origin in the geometric square.

questions.question: The fourth power of a number was called
questions.explanation: Varga-varga (square of the square) is the fourth power. Varga-mula and ghana-mula mean square root and cube root.

questions.question: Why is the word 'root' used for the mathematical operation √?
options: The Arabic word jidhr simply means 'a whole number'
Sanskrit mula, a plant's root, was also used for roots
Roots of plants branch out in square-shaped patterns
The Latin word radix originally meant 'a square figure'
questions.explanation: Mula meant root, basis, origin. Arabic (jidhr) and Latin (radix) later copied this plant-root metaphor.

questions.question: Varga-mula and ghana-mula mean, respectively,
questions.explanation: Mula = root; varga = square; ghana = cube. So varga-mula is the square root and ghana-mula the cube root.

questions.question: The Arabic and Latin words that copied the Sanskrit use of mula for 'root' are
questions.explanation: Arabic jidhr and Latin radix both mean the root of a plant and were used for mathematical roots. Pada is another Sanskrit word for root.

questions.question: Aryabhata (499 CE) stated that
options: the product of two equal quantities is also called varga
the pada of a krti is that of which it is a square
1729 is the sum of two cubes in two different ways
every perfect square is a sum of consecutive odd numbers
questions.explanation: Aryabhata: 'A square figure of four equal sides and the number representing its area are called varga. The product of two equal quantities is also called varga.' The pada statement is Brahmagupta's.

questions.question: Brahmagupta (628 CE) explained that
options: mula, the root of a plant, is also used for the square root
the pada (root) of a krti (square) is that of which it is a square
a varga is a square figure of four equal sides and its area
a ghana is both a solid cube and the third power of a number
questions.explanation: Brahmagupta's definition of the root uses pada (foot, basis): the root of a square is the number of which it is the square. The varga definition belongs to Aryabhata.

questions.question: The terms varga and ghana were used in India at least from the third century CE.
questions.explanation: False. They were used at least from the third century BCE — several hundred years earlier than 'CE' would suggest.

questions.question: Which of these words were used for a mathematical ROOT? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Mula and pada both meant root (basis, origin). Varga and krti mean square, and ghana means cube.
